messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Kofi's Story

Kofi Mensah had been designing curricula for a mid-sized education nonprofit for nearly twelve years when the traffic stop changed everything. It was a Tuesday evening in March, just after six o'clock, when he was pulled over on Martin Luther King Boulevard—a stretch of road he drove three times a week on his way home to his wife, Ama, and their two teenage children. The officer approached his window, and Kofi, a meticulous man who had always believed in doing everything correctly, produced his license and registration immediately. He was polite, even deferential. But something in the officer's tone—a sharpness, a suspicion that seemed unmoored from anything Kofi had actually done—made his chest tighten. The officer asked him to step out of the vehicle. Then came the frisk, the aggressive pat-down, the feeling of being treated as a threat in his own body. Kofi remembered the officer's hand pressing hard against his ribs, remembered the heat rising in his face, the sense of powerlessness that flooded through him as a second officer arrived and the first one's voice grew louder, more authoritative. It lasted perhaps four minutes. No citation was issued. No explanation was given. When Kofi was finally allowed back to his car, his hands were shaking so badly he could barely grip the steering wheel.

In the weeks that followed, Kofi noticed a shift in his nervous system that he couldn't quite control. Loud noises—a car backfiring, a door slamming at work—would send a jolt through his body that left him breathless. At home, he found himself constantly aware of sounds outside, of headlights sweeping across the bedroom window at night. His coworkers began to comment, gently, that he seemed on edge. One afternoon in April, a colleague approached his desk to ask about a lesson plan revision, and Kofi's entire body went rigid; his heart raced as though he were back on that roadside, as though the threat were immediate and real. He apologized, embarrassed, but the incident unsettled him. He was hypervigilant in ways that felt both necessary and exhausting—scanning parking lots before entering them, noting the positions of people around him, calculating exits from rooms.

It was the intrusion of the memory itself that proved most destabilizing. The physical sensations would return without warning—the pressure of hands on his ribs, the heat in his face—and with them came an emotional intensity so overwhelming that Kofi would have to excuse himself, sometimes from meetings, sometimes from conversations with Ama. What made it worse was that the memory rarely came as a coherent narrative. He could not articulate it in sequence; when he tried to tell Ama what had happened, the words scattered. Instead, fragments would ambush him: the officer's jaw, the metallic smell of the patrol car, the sensation of powerlessness. Sometimes he would feel the full force of the terror and shame without any image at all, just a crushing weight in his chest that made him certain something catastrophic was about to occur. The heightened vigilance that now governed his daily life—the constant monitoring for threat—seemed to keep the memory close, as though his nervous system believed that if he remained alert enough, he could prevent the moment from returning. But the opposite was happening. The more he scanned for danger, the more his mind replayed the traffic stop, and the more he replayed it, the more his body reacted as though it were happening again.

By June, Kofi had begun to avoid driving on Martin Luther King Boulevard altogether, taking a longer route home that added twenty minutes to his commute. He avoided situations where he might encounter police—he no longer drove after dark if he could help it, and he had stopped attending community events in neighborhoods where police presence was visible. His children asked why he seemed distant, why he was always checking his phone, why he no longer came to their school events. Ama noticed that he was sleeping poorly, that he would wake in the night drenched in sweat, that intimacy between them had become impossible because his body could not relax. The work that had once brought him satisfaction—designing curricula about civic engagement and social justice—now felt hollow, even triggering. How could he teach students about their rights when he no longer believed his own were protected?

It was Ama who finally insisted he seek help. She told him, with a firmness born of love and desperation, that she could not watch him disappear into fear. Kofi came to his first appointment carrying the weight of three months of sleeplessness, hypervigilance, and a memory that would not cohere into words but that lived in his body nonetheless. What he feared most was that this state—this constant readiness for catastrophe, this fragmentation of mind and body—would become permanent. What he hoped for, though he could barely articulate it, was to feel safe in his own skin again.
